While I agree with you in general - far too often AI is assumed to essentially be a very long list of if-then-else evaluation, which is very often not the case with modern AI - if the article is accurate, then in this case, skepticism of this kind is warranted.

The idea of producing solutions genetically is an excellent one, if you a) have a heuristic that's good, and b) do not have a moving target in terms of "what makes a good solution," in which case the criteria of the heuristic being good changes along with the problem domain.

Unlike a neural net, a genetic algorithm (which, possibly in concert with genetic programming, is probably the basis for how one generates a genetic fuzzy tree, the core data structure of the AI according to the article) produces a static solution to the problem. Fuzzy logic lets it treat cases in a more sophisticated manner than simple if-then-else processing, but ultimately the overall criteria are rigid once the tree is produced. As such, it's possible to beat the AI if you can find weaknesses in the tree, and I seriously doubt that the AI can afford to rebuild its core data structure on the fly, even assuming that the new tree will be an improvement, which is not guaranteed. Google's AI, that you linked to, is a neural network, so far as I can tell from a cursory search: https://deepmind.com/research/dqn/ and so it's far more likely to be able to address rapidly changing circumstances.

Put something in there that actually adjusts performance on the fly, though, and then we're talking adaptable.
